explain.say: Next time you see a row of hills, look carefully. The near ones are dark green, but the far ones look pale, blue and fuzzy, almost like a ghost. Why? Look at the board. The first reason is that air is in the way.

explain.say: Air looks invisible, but it is full of tiny bits that bounce blue light around, the same reason the sky is blue. The more air between you and a hill, the more blue gets added. Look at the second reason. Have you noticed this on a long car or train journey?

explain.say: Artists copy this to make a flat painting feel deep. Look at the board: near hills get strong, warm colours and sharp edges; far hills get pale, cool blue-grey and soft edges. This is called aerial perspective. Which side would you paint first?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Fade, cool and blur things to push them back

explain.say: Brilliant looking! Wow fact: Leonardo da Vinci wrote about this effect and used blue, misty hills behind the Mona Lisa, and Chinese landscape painters have shown mountains fading into mist for over a thousand years. Challenge: paint three hills, each one paler and bluer than the last.

faq.a: Aerial, or atmospheric, perspective is a way of showing distance by making far things paler, bluer and less detailed, just as the air makes them look in real life.
asks: Why do artists make backgrounds blue?

faq.a: Air scatters short, blue light waves more than red ones, so the more air between you and something, the more blue light is added to what you see.
asks: Why do mountains look blue far away?

faq.a: Make far things smaller, paler, cooler and blurrier, with less contrast, and keep strong colours, darks and sharp details for the front of the picture.
asks: How do I make a painting look deep?
How to paint mountains far away

faq.a: Leonardo da Vinci described it and used it in the Mona Lisa's background, and Chinese ink painters used layers of mist and fading mountains centuries earlier.
asks: How do Chinese paintings show distance?

faq.q: Is aerial perspective the same as linear perspective?
faq.a: No. Linear perspective uses lines and vanishing points to make things smaller with distance; aerial perspective uses colour, contrast and blur. Artists often use both.
asks: Two kinds of perspective in art

facts: Air scatters blue light more strongly than red light, which is also why the sky looks blue.
Leonardo da Vinci described atmospheric perspective in his notebooks.
